messages.subject: Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
parts:
Hi list,

I'm trying to code the state-space representation of the JS model for capture-mark-recapture data in stan and I think I've reached the (current) limit of my mathematical ability with regards to marginalization of the (latent) discrete parameter.

The basic model is represented by three Bernoulli sampling statements.

i corresponds to observed individual, t is the point in time, p is sampling/observation probability, y_{i,t} is the observed state (0 or 1), z is the latent discrete state (0 or 1), phi is the probability of survival from t to t+1, and gamma is the probability of being "born" (recruitment).  There are no "zombies" (individuals can't be reborn).

y_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(p_{t} * z_{i,t})
z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(z_{i,t-1} * phi_{t-1} + (1 - z{i,t-1}) * gamma_{t})
z_{i,1} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{1}).

Note that I can also write z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{t} + (phi_{t} - gamma{t}) * z_{i,t}) instead of the second sampling statement following Royle and Dorazio's "Hierarchical modeling and inference in ecology" book. I've also attached a relevant 2012 paper from King titled "A review of Bayesian state-space modelling of capture–recapture–recovery data". The most relevant section is 2.2 (Estimating abundance).

Given that I want to implement this in stan, I need to marginalize out the discrete parameter z. This is where me problem comes in: I don't know how to do this.

I've read over the CJS model implemented in the stan manual (page 111), and it has been quite helpful for better understanding what I'd probably have to do. I'm just stuck on how to modify that to end with the JS model via the introduction of recruitment.

Any advice would be highly appreciated.

Cheers,

Peter Smits

> y_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(p_{t} * z_{i,t})
> z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(z_{i,t-1} * phi_{t-1} + (1 - z{i,t-1}) * gamma_{t})
> z_{i,1} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{1}).

Here's the way to think about this:

p(y, z, phi, p, gamma)

= p(phi, p, gamma) // prior

* PROD_{i in 1:N} bern(z[i,1] | gamma[1])

* PROD_{t in 2:T} bern(z[i,t] | z[i,t-1] * phi[t-1] + (1 - z[i, t-1]) * gamma[t])

* bern(y[i,t] | p[t] * z[i,t])

Then the goal is to marginalize out the the parameter z[i,t] representing if
individual i is alive at time t to get:

p(y, phi, p, gamma)

It's both tricky and tractable because of the constraints, which I would
think should ensure that z[i,] must be a sequence of contiguous 1s that
includes all t such that y[i,t] = 1.

* if y[i,t] = 1 then z[i,t] = 1

* if z[i,t] = 0 and any z[i,t-1] = 1, then z[i, t + n ] = 0 for all n > 0

In words, z[i,] has to be a sequence of contiguous 1s that includes
all t such that y[i,t] = 1.

So what you need to do is add all the probability for the legal z configurations
together (of which there are luckily at most T^2 due to constraints).

This is quite a bit trickier to code than the one in the manual, but has the
same principle. You want to define a function

// compute log likelihood of y for a single individual
real state_space_log(int[] y, vector phi, vector p, vector gamma) {
i.e., big sum (using log-sum-exp) over legal z values
vector[first_sighting[i] * (T - last_sighting[i])] lp;
int i;
i <- 0;
for (t_first_alive in 1:first_siting[i]) {
for (t_last_alive in (last_siting[i] + 1):T) {
log_prob[i] <- log prob for config, which involves more looping,
but now z[i,t] == (t >= t_first_alive && t <= t_last_alive)
i <- i + 1;
return log_sum_exp(log_prob);
}

It'll probably help to create an auxliary data structure of first and last
sightings, because you know it has to be all 1s before that, so then there's
just the choice of when the individual was born (which can be before the
first time point --- that's gamma[1], right?) and when the individual died (which
can be after the last time point).

And then the model is super simple.

for (i in 1:I)
y[i] ~ state_space(phi, p, gamma);

Sorry it's such a hassle! If there's only 30 time periods and 1000 individuals, it
should be tractable enough to sample.

If this isn't enough of a hint, I can help out more. I'm going to send
a different message with my implementation of the Dorazio-Royle species-site
occupancy model, which involves another marginalization. I really want

same principle.  You want to define a function

The key is this simple relation:

p(a) = SUM_b p(a,b)

To make a simpler case, let's say you have 5 observation times
and have observed the animal at time=2 and time=3, that is,

observed captures y: 01100

Then you get the following options for z

01100 first_alive=2 last_alive=3
01110
01111
11100
11110
11111 first_alive=1 last_alive=5

And what you need to do is compute p(y,z) for each of these z
on the log scale in an array,

lp[1] = log p(y=01100, z=01100 | p, phi, gamma)
lp[2] = log p(y=01100, z=01110 | p, phi, gamma)
...
lp[6] = log p(y=01100, z=11111 | p, phi, gamma)

then use:

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));

because

log_sum_exp(lp) = log (exp(lp[1]) + exp(lp[2]) + ... + exp(lp[6]))

= log (p[1] + ... p[6])

where p[1] = exp(lp[1]) is the probability of y and the first config of z.

So you take the sum of the probabilities of each pair of y and legal z
and add them up then take the log. It's just log_sum_exp does it more
efficiently and has more arithmetic stability and accuracy.

The trick is that you're going to need to do this in a double loop over
first_alive and last_alive.

but when that's done, I'll implement the model and do some data

parts:
The answer I gave you before was right, but inefficient.

Reading Ruth King's paper made me think about the whole model
as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in
the Stan Manual's CJS model for the probability of being uncaptured (not sighted)
after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
algorithm. By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
alive at t.

Then, given first[i] as first sighting of i and last[i] as last sighting
of i, we can use the forward value up to first[i] and backward value back
to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1
(the individual can't die and come back to life between first[i] and last[i]).

So I'd probably write this as a likelihood function for y conditioned on
a whole bunch of things:

real
log_likelihood(int[] y, // observations
int first, // first sighting time
int last, // last sighting time
vector alpha, // in study at first sighting
vector chi, // unsighted after last sighting
vector phi, // survive from t to t+1
vector p) { // sighted given alive
real ll;
ll <- alpha[first] + chi[last];
for (t in first:(last-1))
ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t]);
for (t in first:last)
ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(y[t], p[t]);
return ll;
}

The first loop is that it survives from each point to the next
point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond
last, which is why phi[last] isn't included). The second loop just
takes the sighting/capture probabilities for each point.

The first, last, and alpha values all get computed as in the previous model.
I'd define first and last as transformed data so as not to have to recompute.

Im assuming alpha and chi are defined on the log scale.

You can then define alpha and chi as locals in the model block, where
b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.

alpha[1] <- log(b[1]);
for (t in 2:T)
alpha[t] <- log_sum_exp(alpha[t-1] + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t-1]),
b[t]);

The log_sum_exp is for the mixture of either being in the study at time t-1
and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.

Moving on to the abundance study, you'll also have a bunch of individuals
who were never sighted. So you have to increment the log density by the
probability of that, too. Which is another calculation like the others,
because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they
are in the study, they are unobserved.

I think that's it. Let me know if you have more questions.

This is fun! Especially when I don't have to debug it all. You
really want to check all the boundary conditions in the above to make
sure they're right.

- Bob

> as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in

> after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
> algorithm. By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
> that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
> alive at t.

> to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1

> log_likelihood(int[] y, // observations
> int first, // first sighting time
> int last, // last sighting time
> vector alpha, // in study at first sighting
> vector chi, // unsighted after last sighting
> vector phi, // survive from t to t+1

> point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond

> b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.
>

> b[t]);

> and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.

> who were never sighted. So you have to increment the log density by the
> probability of that, too. Which is another calculation like the others,
> because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they

You're right. Looking log_sum_exp(lp) where lp is a vector of log probabilities, it sometimes has a value of -inf. 

I think the issue is the definition of lp. it is defined vector[first_capture(y) * (size(y) - last_capture(y))] lp; What happens, is that if last_capture is equal to size(y) the vector has length 0. And that is bad. This causes further problems when trying to loop from (last_capture + 1):size(y). 

So, I add 1 to the length of the vector lp, then it is no longer degenerate in the case where last_capture(y) == size(y). I then also changef the t_last_alive loop to last_capture:S. This seems to have fixed it.

As long as there's no undefined variables floating around.

I'd think what you want to do is this:

vector[first_capture(y) * max(size(y) - last_capture(y), 1)] ...;

BUT, that runs into a bug we have in using max() within bounds
that I'm currently in the process of fixing. So you'll have to do it like
this:

vector[foo(first_capture(y), size(y), last_capture(y))] ...;

with

int foo(int fc, int s, int lc) {
return fc * max(1, s - lc);
}

The fix for max in vector declarations probably won't make it into
Stan 2.7.0, which we're trying to rush out the door to deal
with BH (Boost headers) changing versions on us so that nobody can
get RStan to build.

> > > On Friday, May 29, 2015 at 4:31:56 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > The answer I gave you before was right, but inefficient.
> > >
> > > Reading Ruth King's paper made me think about the whole model
> > > as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in
> > > the Stan Manual's CJS model for the probability of being uncaptured (not sighted)
> > > after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
> > > algorithm. By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
> > > that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
> > > alive at t.
> > >
> > > Then, given first[i] as first sighting of i and last[i] as last sighting
> > > of i, we can use the forward value up to first[i] and backward value back
> > > to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1
> > > (the individual can't die and come back to life between first[i] and last[i]).
> > >
> > > So I'd probably write this as a likelihood function for y conditioned on
> > > a whole bunch of things:
> > >
> > > real
> > > log_likelihood(int[] y, // observations
> > > int first, // first sighting time
> > > int last, // last sighting time
> > > vector alpha, // in study at first sighting
> > > vector chi, // unsighted after last sighting
> > > vector phi, // survive from t to t+1
> > > vector p) { // sighted given alive
> > > real ll;
> > > ll <- alpha[first] + chi[last];
> > > for (t in first:(last-1))
> > > ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t]);
> > > for (t in first:last)
> > > ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(y[t], p[t]);
> > > return ll;
> > > }
> > >
> > > The first loop is that it survives from each point to the next
> > > point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond
> > > last, which is why phi[last] isn't included). The second loop just
> > > takes the sighting/capture probabilities for each point.
> > >
> > > The first, last, and alpha values all get computed as in the previous model.
> > > I'd define first and last as transformed data so as not to have to recompute.
> > >
> > > Im assuming alpha and chi are defined on the log scale.
> > >
> > > You can then define alpha and chi as locals in the model block, where
> > > b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.
> > >
> > > alpha[1] <- log(b[1]);
> > > for (t in 2:T)
> > > alpha[t] <- log_sum_exp(alpha[t-1] + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t-1]),
> > > b[t]);
> > >
> > > The log_sum_exp is for the mixture of either being in the study at time t-1
> > > and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.
> > >
> > > Moving on to the abundance study, you'll also have a bunch of individuals
> > > who were never sighted. So you have to increment the log density by the
> > > probability of that, too. Which is another calculation like the others,
> > > because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they
> > > are in the study, they are unobserved.
> > >
